newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: PALM OIL - Asian prices seen locked in tight range.
newsitem.headline: PALM OIL - Asian prices seen locked in tight range.

text.p: Asian palm oil prices are seen trading in a range this week due to year-end festivities, but the Indonesian market may hold steady owing to relatively high prices, regional traders said.

Traders in Singapore said a seasonal shortage in ships to transport vegetable oil produced in Malaysia and Indonesia to the United States and Europe was expected to keep the regional market in a tight range.
"Many ships seem reluctant to come here to lift the oil, but this always happens at this time of the year," said a Singaporean trader.
Ample supply of competing edible oils from South America, supported by the United States, should also keep the Asian market range-bound, Singapore traders said.
"It's going to be flat," said a Singapore-based dealer for a U.S. commodity house. "It's a real Christmas market. Everybody's getting ready for the holidays."
"There are no leads in the market to talk about. It's going to drift," another dealer on the island-state said.
Malaysian palm oil traders said they were expecting statistics on output and export for end-November from the state Palm Oil Registration and Licensing Authority (PORLA).
"The next key data will only be PORLA data, and that is on December 16," a trader said. "In the meanwhile, we expect some fresh tenders from big buyers like India and Pakistan."
On Friday, Malaysian private crop forecaster Ivan Wong estimated that November output fell 14 percent to 764,000 tonnes over October, while end-November stocks stood at 965,000 tonnes.
Third position February contract on the Kuala Lumpur Commodities Exchange will probably trade in a range between 1,210-1,230 ringgit a tonne, traders said.
The contract closed on Friday at 1,193 ringgit.
"February futures contract is expected to hover around 1,200 ringgit level in the short-term," a trader in Kuala Lumpur said.
"The contract has been trading within a 20-ringgit range in recent weeks and we need some strong market influencing factors to give the market a clear path," he added.
"It won't really go out of that range unless something comes up," a dealer in Singapore said, commenting on the February futures in Malaysia.

In Indonesia, traders said sentiment was expected to be helped by the warning from Beddu Amang, chief of state logistics agency BULOG, who said exporters and producers would complain if palm olein prices dipped below 1,400 rupiah/kg.
Amang also said the olein prices should not exceed 1,500 rupiah before the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan in January.
"His statement seems to indicate that BULOG will not intervene in the market at current prices," a trader in Indonesia said.
"It will provide a psychological boost as players can now rest assured BULOG will not intervene at the moment," said the trader.
Indonesian palm olein finished last week at 1,400-05 rupiah/kg, compared with 1,435-30 rupiah previously.
Crude palm oil was quoted at around 1,209 rupiah/kg in the North Sumatran city of Medan, against 1,222 a week ago.
"Crude palm oil prices are still relatively high, so I think olein prices will have to adjust higher," another Indonesian trader said. "At the moment, there is no processing margin at all."
(with contributions from K.T. Arasu from Jakarta and Rene Pastor from Singapore)
